PMGT1865 Week 04

PMGT1865 Week 04 — PERT and Duration Uncertainty

Purpose and Three-Point Estimates

The Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT) uses three estimates of each activity's duration to represent uncertainty and approximate the probability of finishing within a target duration.

Symbol

Definition

a

Optimistic duration: a favourable estimate

m

Most likely duration: the estimate judged most probable

b

Pessimistic duration: an unfavourable estimate

tₑ

Expected activity duration

σᵢ

Estimated standard deviation of activity i's duration

σᵢ²

Estimated variance of activity i's duration

μ

Expected duration of the selected critical path

σₚ

Standard deviation of that path's total duration

T

Target elapsed completion time

z

Target's distance from the expected duration in standard-deviation units

Φ(z)

Standard normal cumulative probability up to z

Use consistent time units and estimates satisfying a ≤ m ≤ b. Variance has squared time units; standard deviation has the same time units as duration.

Activity and Project Formulas

Quantity

Formula

Expected activity duration

tₑ = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6

Activity standard deviation

σᵢ = (b − a) ÷ 6

Activity variance

σᵢ² = ((b − a) ÷ 6)²

Expected critical-path duration

μ = Σ tₑ along the selected critical path

Critical-path variance, assuming independent durations

σₚ² = Σ σᵢ² along that path

Critical-path standard deviation

σₚ = √(Σ σᵢ²)

Standardised target

z = (T − μ) ÷ σₚ

Approximate completion probability

P(completion by T) ≈ Φ(z)

The sum symbol Σ means to add the indicated values. The project mean is also sometimes written TE; tₑ refers to an individual activity here.

• A positive z means the target is later than the expected duration.

• A negative z means it is earlier.

• z = 0 corresponds to approximately 50% completion probability under the normal approximation.

• A target time for probability p can be estimated as T = μ + zₚσₚ, where Φ(zₚ) = p.

Calculation Method

Define the network and obtain a, m and b for every activity.

Calculate each expected duration and variance.

Use the expected durations in a critical-path calculation. The critical path is the longest logical start-to-finish path for those durations.

Add expected durations and variances along that path, then take the square root of the variance sum.

Calculate z for the target time and evaluate Φ(z).

Interpret the probability in light of the independence, path-selection and distribution assumptions.

Keep full precision until the final display unless deliberately demonstrating a specified rounding convention.

Worked Example — Three Activities and a 14-Day Target

A precedes both B and C, with finish-to-start links and zero lag. The project completes only after both branches finish. All duration estimates are in days.

Step 1: Calculate Activity Estimates

Activity

a

m

b

Expected duration tₑ

Standard deviation

Variance

A

(3 + 4 × 5 + 9) ÷ 6 = 32/6 = 5.3333

(9 − 3) ÷ 6 = 1

(10 − 4) ÷ 6 = 1

The decimal values shown are rounded for display; calculations below use the fractions.

Step 2: Compare the Paths

Path

Expected duration

A → B

32/6 + 38/6 = 70/6 = 11.6667 days

A → C

32/6 + 26/6 = 58/6 = 9.6667 days

A → B is the critical path based on expected durations. Thus μ = 70/6 ≈ 11.67 days.

Step 3: Calculate Project Uncertainty

For A → B:

• σₚ² = 1 + 1 = 2 days².

• σₚ = √2 ≈ 1.4142 days.

C's variance is not included in this selected-path approximation. This does not mean that uncertainty on the other branch can never affect actual completion.

Step 4: Calculate the Completion Probability

For T = 14 days:

z = (14 − 70/6) ÷ √2 ≈ 1.6499.

Φ(1.6499) ≈ 0.95052, giving an approximate 95.05% probability of completing by day 14 under the selected-path normal approximation. A normal table using z rounded to 1.65 gives approximately 95.05% as well.

Strengths and Limitations

• Three-point estimates make uncertainty explicit rather than hiding it inside a single duration.

• The formulas support a structured comparison of completion targets and schedule risk.

• The estimates remain judgement-dependent; optimistic and pessimistic durations are not guaranteed bounds.

• Adding variances assumes independent activity durations. Shared causes can make durations correlated.

• A normal approximation may be weak for short paths or strongly skewed durations.

• A non-critical or near-critical branch may become the longest path when actual durations vary. A fixed-path approximation can therefore overstate completion probability.

• Resource constraints, calendar restrictions and changing dependencies require additional schedule modelling; the probability calculation does not resolve them automatically.
